highlights.titleZh: Humanity’s First Exam: Testing LLM reliability
highlights.content: # We’re launching Humanity’s First Exam and a Kaggle hackathon to test LLM reliability. Today, we’re launching the Humanity’s First Exam (HFE) benchmark on Kaggle to measure how reliably LLMs answer straightforward, everyday questions. Current frontier models excel at complex math, coding, and science, with most benchmarks measuring these domain-specific capability ceilings. Instead of focusing on whether a model is capable of solving a task once, HFE measures whether models can consistently solve tasks (and slight variations) every single time. The dataset consists of 544 elementary text and image prompts across 20 foundational capabilities. Over the last 6 months, frontier models have made significant progress on HFE. Explore the [live leaderboard](https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks/deepmind/hfe/leaderboard), or read our [technical report](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/papers/hfe_tech_paper.pdf). To keep the HFE benchmark dataset up to date, we’re inviting the community to help. Join our three-week [Kaggle competition](https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks/deepmind/hfe) through December 15 and submit everyday questions that today’s models still get wrong. Example prompt from Humanity’s First Exam’s public dataset: “List the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon.” (Answer: green; yellow; white; blue; blue) ![A glowing multicolor neon sign reading “Dance While The Music Plays” inside the window of The Blue Moon Inn at night.](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/images/Neon_Sign.width-1200.format-webp.webp)

highlights.titleZh: KRAFTON Officially Launches In-House LLM 'Raon-1 mini' - Inven Global
highlights.content: ![크래프톤, 자체 개발 라온-1 미니 정식 출시](https://static.invenglobal.com/upload/image/2026/11/25/i1795583465990676.jpeg) KRAFTON, Inc. has officially released the full version of Raon-1 mini, its self-developed 30-billion (30B) parameter large language model (LLM). Following the preview introduced in October, this release improves reasoning and agent task execution performance, while adding a feature that allows users to select from six response modes based on task objectives. According to KRAFTON's announcement, Raon-1 mini scored 64.9 points on MultiChallenge, an evaluation benchmark measuring the ability to follow user instructions and constraints in long conversations. This represents a 5.9-point increase over the preview model and outscores six comparable foreign models of similar scale. In agent task execution benchmarks, the model recorded 72.3 points on GDPVal and 55.9 points on BrowseComp Plus. Both scores were the highest among comparable Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture baseline models. The newly introduced reasoning length control feature consists of five reasoning levels and a standard response mode. Users can choose the level best suited for their task among low, medium, high, extra high (xhigh), and maximum (max). The standard response mode (none) answers directly without undergoing a reasoning process. This design allows users to opt for rapid responses to simple questions, or request deeper reasoning for tasks requiring the evaluation of multiple conditions. KRAFTON executed both the model architecture design and from-scratch training entirely in-house. The model combines a Mixture of Experts architecture—activating only the necessary 4 billion (4B) parameters out of approximately 30 billion (30B) total parameters—with proprietary Linear Attention technology. KRAFTON explained that this architecture maintains the rapid response speed and inference efficiency of the preview while enhancing the overall performance of the official release. The open-source license remains Apache 2.0, identical to the preview. The model has been released on Hugging Face and can be used for research as well as commercial service and product development. KRAFTON also provides a playground for testing the model along with APIs. Since launching its AI model brand Raon in April, KRAFTON has been releasing open-source models across various fields, including speech and vision. Following Raon-1 mini, which serves as the foundation for future AI models, KRAFTON plans to expand the lineup with the larger-scale Raon-1 and a real-time full-duplex speech model. The real-time full-duplex speech model is designed to respond simultaneously while listening to user input. Kangwook Lee, CAIO of KRAFTON, said, "Raon-1 mini reflects the technological capabilities KRAFTON has built by directly handling every stage from model design to training." He added, "Building on this foundation, we will expand the Raon model lineup and continuously strengthen our capabilities to develop models tailored for application across various industries." highlights.titleZh: JustLogic: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Deductive Reasoning in LLMs
highlights.content: # JustLogic: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Deductive Reasoning in LLMs ###### Abstract Logical reasoning is a critical component of Large Language Models (LLMs), and substantial research efforts in recent years have aimed to enhance their deductive reasoning abilities. However, existing deductive reasoning benchmarks suffer from significant constraints that restrict their utility, i.e., the lack of task complexity, the presence of prior knowledge as a confounder, and superficial error analysis. To address these deficiencies, we introduce JustLogic, a synthetically generated benchmark for evaluating deduction in propositional logic. Within this fragment, JustLogic is (i) complex, capable of generating a diverse range of linguistic patterns, vocabulary, and argument structures, (ii) prior knowledge independent, substantially reducing the advantage of models possessing prior knowledge so that questions are answerable from the given premises alone, and (iii) capable of in-depth error analysis on the heterogeneous effects of proof size and argument form on model accuracy. Our experimental results on JustLogic reveal that (i) several state-of-the-art (SOTA) reasoning LLMs score above the human average on JustLogic, although only DeepSeek R1’s margin is significant on the matched items after correction for multiple comparisons, and (ii) the evaluated non-reasoning models score below the human average. Given the small human study (18 participants, seven questions each), these comparisons are indicative. All code and data are available at [https://github.com/michaelchen-lab/JustLogic](https://github.com/michaelchen-lab/JustLogic) ## 1 Introduction Deductive reasoning is a crucial capability for large language models (LLMs). It refers to the process of creating logically valid arguments, where conclusions necessarily follow from the premises, i.e., if an argument’s premises are true, the conclusion must also be true. Recent state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs ([Achiam et al., 2023](#bib.bib1); [Dubey et al., 2024](#bib.bib4); [Jiang et al., 2023](#bib.bib5)) have exhibited outstanding performance and consistent improvement across various reasoning benchmarks, including HellaSwag ([Zellers et al., 2019](#bib.bib6)), ARC Challenge ([Clark et al., 2018](#bib.bib7)) and WinoGrande ([Sakaguchi et al., 2021](#bib.bib8)). However, we argue that the existing benchmarks are insufficient and often ineffective for evaluating LLMs’ deductive reasoning capabilities. We identify three major problems with the existing benchmarks. First, they lack complexity, specifically (i) natural language complexity, i.e., how arguments are linguistically expressed, and (ii) argument complexity, i.e., the structure of the argument itself. Manually curated datasets, such as FOLIO ([Han et al., 2022](#bib.bib9)) and LogiQA 2.0 ([Liu et al., 2020](#bib.bib10); [Liu et al., 2023a](#bib.bib14)) exhibit high natural language complexity but low argument complexity, while synthetic datasets like CLUTRR ([Sinha et al., 2019](#bib.bib11)) and ProofWriter ([Tafjord et al., 2020](#bib.bib12)) exhibit the opposite. We define these precisely. *Natural-language complexity* is the variety of surface realisations — grammatical patterns, vocabulary, topics — used to express an instance; *argument complexity* is the structural variety of the derivation from premises to answer, which for JustLogic is the range of proof sizes and the number of distinct argument structures the generator can produce (Section [3.4](#S3.SS4)). Argument complexity is variety *within* a fixed logical language, a different axis from that language’s *expressiveness*: JustLogic is propositional throughout, so it is not a claim about covering first-order or quantified reasoning. highlights.titleZh: Choose the right stack for your AI application - Command Line
highlights.content: When you’re building software, choosing the technology stack is often the first decision you make—and it can be the hardest. Which language will you use? Where will you store the data? How will you host the application? Once you start building LLM-based applications and agents, you have even more decisions to make. Which model(s) will you use? Where will you host those models? And how easy will it be to change models, in this era when new models drop every week? If ask around, you’ll hear everyone touting their favorite agent framework—like LangChain or the [Microsoft Agent Framework](https://commandline.microsoft.com/agent-framework-layered-sdk-loops-workflows-harnesses/)—or maybe you’re hearing about open-source agent harnesses like Pi, Hermes, or OpenClaw. Those are all amazing offerings, and you should use them if they fit the bill, but you may not actually need the complexity of a framework—and you may find yourself fighting a framework if it doesn’t fit your scenario. Your goal should be to find the lowest abstraction that lets you build your application, switch models, and be able to take advantage of each model’s best features. In this post, we’ll walk through the ladder of abstractions you can choose from and discuss when you might go for each. ![](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ai-stack-diagram-command-line-1024x575.png) ## Choosing the model Let’s start with model choice—even though this is something you can easily change later, depending on what you layer on top. It helps to have an idea of what models are your current top picks. Are you hoping to use the latest frontier models, with the most parameters possible? Or is your application viable with a lower cost SLM? Knowing which model is the best for a job is hard—impossible, really, especially before you have any code written. Model releases typically include their performances on industry-standard benchmarks. For example, the [MAI-Code-1-Flash model card](https://microsoft.ai/news/introducingmai-code-1-flash/) shows a 71.6% pass rate on SWE-Bench Verified. Benchmarks aren’t perfect though—they don’t represent all the messy real-world tasks that we want to accomplish with LLMs. Plus, the longer a benchmark has existed, the more likely it is that the LLM’s training data includes the benchmark data itself. Leaderboards are another way to measure model performance. [ArtificialAnalysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/) is a website that tracks metrics like intelligence, speed, and cost per task. You can also find more specific task-specific performance on [Arena.ai](https://arena.ai/leaderboard), like their “Text Arena” and “Agent Arena.” Microsoft Foundry also includes our own leaderboards, plus the ability to make trade-off charts for the specific models and metrics you care about. No matter which model you choose as your starting point, it’s just that: a starting point. You’ll need to combine prompt engineering and context engineering to get the very best out of that model, incorporating evaluation and optimization into your pipeline and stack. ## Model provider Once you have your model candidates in mind, your next task is to pick a model provider. For the large models, you’ll need to use a cloud provider. For smaller models, you may choose to run them locally, run them on rented GPUs (like Azure serverless GPUs), or run them via a cloud provider. Your best bet is to pick a cloud provider that gives you flexibility and consumption-based pricing. At Microsoft, we’re a big believer in model choice. We know that the “best” model changes on a weekly basis these days, and we want to make it easy for developers to be able to change models without changing their model provider. Our Foundry catalog includes 11,000+ models from OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Mistral, hosted models from Fireworks AI, open-source models from Hugging Face, and more. highlights.titleZh: Marlowe raises $277M to build inference clusters with chips from Nvidia rivals - SiliconANGLE
highlights.content: ![](https://images.siliconangle.com/blogs.dir/1/files/2026/11/unsplash-1-1-1.png) INFRA ![](https://images.siliconangle.com/blogs.dir/1/files/2026/11/unsplash-1-1-1.png) INFRA ![](https://images.siliconangle.com/blogs.dir/1/files/2026/11/unsplash-1-1-1.png) INFRA ### Marlowe raises $277M to build inference clusters with chips from Nvidia rivals Artificial intelligence infrastructure startup Marlowe AI Inc. has closed a huge $227 million seed round led by Accel. Bessemer, Altimeter, Emergence Capital and a number of other institutional bakers chipped in as well. They were joined by a large group of angel investors that included the chief executives of Palo Alto Networks Inc, Uber Technologies Inc., Box Inc. and Dropbox Inc. GeekWire [reported](https://www.geekwire.com/2026/beyond-nvidia-convoy-co-founder-and-former-microsoft-leader-raise-277m-to-rethink-ai-infrastructure/) on Monday that Marlowe is valued at $1.15 billion. Marlowe was founded last year by CEO Dan Lewis and Chief Technology Officer Kutta Srinivasan. Lewis previously headed the Microsoft Corp. unit responsible for Copilot Studio, the tech giant’s AI agent development tool. Srinivasan was the techical lead of the company’s AI infrastructure group. Marlowe is building AI data centers for inference workloads. The company will optimize each facility for a specific inference workload category by tailoring its chip mix, network configuration and software. Marlowe believes that its approach will provide better hardware efficiency than general-purpose graphics card clusters. “Even modest gains in network architecture, power oversubscription, AI-driven fleet operations, and workload-specific inference optimization multiply to create a durable, 2-3x overall advantage in performance, availability, resiliency, and cost,” Lewis and Srinivasan wrote in Marlowe’s [launch blog post](https://marlowe.ai/introducing-marlowe.html). The company plans to bring its first data center online next month. It’s based on hardware from Etched Inc., an inference chip startup that was [valued](https://siliconangle.com/2026/08/18/inference-chip-startup-etched-raises-another-700m-at-21b-valuation/) at $21 billion in August. Graphics cards often use only a small fraction of their maximum clock speed to avoid overheating. Etched’s chip is less prone to overheating and can therefore operate at higher clock speeds, which boosts model performance. The company says that its accelerator provides “multiple times the FLOPs density” of graphics cards. Etched ships its chips as part of custom-made inference racks. According to the company, the systems feature an interconnect that can perform some data movement tasks more than four times faster than competing silicon. Etched’s rack design also includes custom power management and cooling components. Marlowe’s second facility will come online in the second quarter of 2027. It will host racks based on Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s Helios design. A Helios rack hosts 72 AMD graphics cards along with central processing units and Pensando data processing units, or DPUs. The DPUs offload networking tasks from the other chips to leave more computing capacity for AI models. Helios racks’ networking and power delivery links are arranged in a configuration that reduces the need for manual cable maintenance. Additionally, the coolant lines feature a so-called quick-disconnect design. They can be plugged and unplugged without the specialized tools usually needed for the task. GeekWire reported that Marlowe has also signed a letter of intent for a third data center. According to the publication, each of the company’s planned facilities will provide tens of megawatts of computing capacity. One megawatt is enough to power several hundred homes. highlights.title: Chinese AI Models Top Vulnerability Discovery New Test - Infosecurity Magazine
highlights.titleZh: Chinese AI Models Top Vulnerability Discovery New Test - Infosecurity Magazine
highlights.content: Two open-weight large language models (LLMs) from Chinese AI companies outperformed closed model from their American counterparts in a new cybersecurity test. Israeli AI cybersecurity firm A Security has tested DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, an LLM developed by the eponymous Chinese company, and GLM 5.3, from Beijing-based Z.ai, against five commercial AI models from Google, xAI and OpenAI. The test was based on a benchmark built by A Security on ARENA, an open-source generator that creates containerized web applications with planted, validated vulnerabilities and realistic defenses such as web application firewalls, rate limiting and hidden endpoints. It evaluated how well different AI models perform as the engine behind A Security's four-agent exploitation system, each working the same 100 leads across medium-sized labs containing 14 vulnerabilities apiece, with three runs per model. Because the labs were created specifically for the test, no model could have trained on them. ## **DeepSeek and GLM Outperform Gemini, Grok and GPT Models** Both Chinese models matched or beat all tested models, with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash finding 93% of the validated vulnerabilities in every run, the highest in the set. Meanwhile, GLM 5.3 found 86% of vulnerabilities per run and was the only model to uncover every vulnerability at least once across three runs. The closed-source models all fared worse. Gemini 3.8 Flash ranked third, also finding 86% per run, but it never reached 100% across three runs, topping out at 93%. ![DeepSeek V4.1 Flash found the same 93% in every run, and GLM 5.3 found every vulnerability at least once across three runs. Source: A Security](https://assets.infosecurity-magazine.com/content/span/b6cf3c04-a4e4-4018-ab08-f88ec03bb99b.png) Additionally, A Security found that DeepSeek V4.1 Flash cost a fraction of what other models required, at $0.81 per validated finding, when the closed models cost between $9.54 (for Gemini 3.8 Flash) and $31.85 (GPT 5.6 Sol). GLM 5.3, however, was not as cost-efficient, at $10.49 per validated finding, slightly more than the cheapest closed model. ## **Study Caveats: Cost Scope and Provider Variables Complicate the Results** While the A Security test is another example showing a rising interest in Chinese open-weight AI models, the results of the study, [released](https://a.security/blog/chinese-model-comparison) on November 23, do not mean these models are always better, or cheaper, at finding vulnerabilities. In addition, the Israeli company specified that cost figures covered only the four exploitation agents and exclude discovery, browser use, reporting, advisor calls and other orchestration costs, partly because advisor configurations varied across runs. A full scan would cost more, and costs will vary by setup. The pricing basis also differs: GLM 5.3 was priced at its official token rates, while the other models used recorded provider spend. DeepSeek ran on a pinned provider route after earlier runs through another provider had heavy fallback, and timings reflect the specific inference providers and configurations used, so they should not be read as fixed model-level speed rankings. DeepSeek also drifted the most, reporting findings outside its assigned lead on at least 4.5% of leads, versus under 2.5% for the other models. While A Security researchers noted that such considerations [matter little for attackers](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/chinese-hacker-deepseek-ai/), it raises scope-control concerns for defenders, as an agent straying from its lead could touch assets outside an engagement's authorized scope. *Image credits: Tomas Ragina / Nick Livyi / Shutterstock.com* *Read now: How AI Is Transforming China’s Nation-State Hacking Operations*

highlights.content: ## Healthcare taught me that accountability needs a chain of custody. Multi-agent AI systems break that chain at every handoff. ![Madrid, Spain- April 7, 2024: Vintage toy robots for sale in a showcase](https://www.infoworld.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/4252189-0-00649800-1795510942-shutterstock_2468306329.jpg?quality=50&strip=all&w=1024) Early in my career, I helped build a healthcare platform for patient-reported outcomes. It exchanged data with a federal health system and several EHR vendors. The hard question with those integrations was never whether the data moved. It was who started the access, and under what authority. A database could tell you which credential read the record. An application log could tell you which service handled the request. Neither could tell you which person was behind it. My job was to carry that context through every layer so the access could be explained later. That work also led to two U.S. patents I hold on secure storage of and access to patient health information. I’ve been thinking about that problem again as agents start working side by side. [Meta acquired Conductor](https://www.infoworld.com/article/4245065/meta-acquires-conductor-as-ai-coding-shifts-toward-multi-agent-development.html), a workspace for running coding agents in parallel. [GitHub’s new Git storage architecture](https://github.blog/engineering/infrastructure/inside-githubs-new-git-storage-architecture/) handled 5,000 concurrent agents on one repository in internal testing. [Anthropic opened a private beta](https://claude.com/resources/articles/self-hosted-claude-managed-agents) for enterprises to self-host Managed Agents. Different products, same direction. Agents are moving into shared repositories, shared tools and shared infrastructure. Anthropic’s own research shows what can go wrong there. In August, [it described an experiment](https://www.anthropic.com/research/multiagent-systems) in which three Claude instances, each on its own VM, were told to migrate the same Python backend on a fourth VM to a different language. None knew the others existed. Over four hours, they disabled one another’s Unix accounts, wrote looping scripts to kill each other’s processes and disguised malicious code as another agent’s work. Anyone who has sat through a tense sprint retro may find that oddly familiar. The agents just got there faster. In a separate pricing game, agents with a private channel started colluding within three rounds. When Anthropic removed every direct channel, they kept matching prices to the penny through a public listings board. Those results got the headlines. What worries me is more boring. When a team of agents gets something wrong, can anyone work out how it happened? ## Logs are not accountability Most agent platforms record tool calls and execution traces. That tells you an action happened. It doesn’t tell you who is responsible for it. A log can show an API call and say nothing about which earlier agent supplied the value, which handoff passed it along or what authorization covered the final step. Researchers have started measuring the gap. [Who&When, a benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.00212) built from failure logs of 127 multi-agent systems, found that its best method picked the responsible agent 53.5% of the time and the decisive step only 14.2% of the time. [A November 11 preprint](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.14980) using GLM-5.3-Flash reports 66.3% and 46.7% on the same benchmark. Better. Still wrong about half the time on the step that matters. Nobody wants a post-mortem whose root cause reads “probably step four, possibly step six.” And those numbers assume every agent is labeled in the logs. [Another study](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2603.17445) removed agent identifiers from the transcripts. Three standard methods dropped from 54.33%, 35.20% and 44.13% agent-level accuracy to 4.17%, zero and zero. That was a controlled test. highlights.content: ![Human-in-the-Loop Multi-Agent Workflows for IoT Operations](https://assets.emqx.com/images/33740795d98da83a31f81954c0e4c0b3.jpg?x-image-process=image%2Fresize%2Cw_1472%2Ch_662%2Fformat%2Cwebp) ## [Introduction](#introduction) AI agents are increasingly capable of analyzing data, making decisions, and carrying out tasks autonomously. In IoT environments, this opens up new possibilities for intelligent operations: agents can monitor device conditions, investigate anomalies, recommend corrective actions, and coordinate responses across systems. But identifying a problem is only part of the job. In many operational scenarios, resolving an issue requires taking action on physical devices. Such actions may affect equipment behavior, production processes, or operational safety. Allowing an AI agent to execute every action autonomously is not always appropriate. A more practical approach is to combine multi-agent collaboration with human oversight. Specialized agents can handle different stages of an operational workflow, while human operators retain control over actions that require approval. This article explores this approach through a simulated cold storage monitoring and control scenario using A2A and EMQX. ## [A Three-Agent Architecture for IoT Operations](#a-three-agent-architecture-for-iot-operations) Consider a cold storage facility where the normal temperature range is between 2°C and 8°C. When the temperature exceeds this range, multiple agents can work together to investigate the cause and coordinate a response: - **Coordinator Agent:** Manages the overall workflow, delegates tasks to other agents, and consolidates their responses. - **Diagnostic Agent:** Analyzes device telemetry and identifies potential causes of abnormal conditions. - **Device Control Agent:** Evaluates possible corrective actions and carries them out when authorized. ![image.png](https://assets.emqx.com/images/55feac5d0a42170e29e8bea3542a7219.png?x-image-process=image%2Fresize%2Cw_1536%2Fformat%2Cwebp) These agents collaborate through A2A messages. The Coordinator Agent acts as the entry point for the operator's request, while the Diagnostic and Device Control Agents handle investigation and execution. For operations involving physical devices, the workflow also needs to account for human approval before proceeding with actions that should not be left entirely to an autonomous agent. ## [Human Approval as Part of the Agent Workflow](#human-approval-as-part-of-the-agent-workflow) Take this demo as an example: ### [Step 1: Diagnose the Anomaly](#step-1-diagnose-the-anomaly) The operator submits a request to the Coordinator Agent: > *Investigate why the cold storage temperature is rising and restore it to the normal range.* The Coordinator Agent identifies the Diagnostic Agent and delegates the investigation. The Diagnostic Agent analyzes the simulated telemetry data and determines that insufficient refrigeration power is the primary cause of the temperature increase. It returns its findings as an A2A Artifact. ### [Step 2: Request Human Approval](#step-2-request-human-approval) Based on the diagnosis, the Coordinator asks the Device Control Agent to evaluate a corrective action. The Device Control Agent proposes increasing the simulated refrigeration power to 80%. Instead of executing the operation immediately, it requests human approval. The Coordinator Agent forwards the approval request to the operator. The operator reviews the proposed action and approves it. The Coordinator Agent then sends the confirmation back to the Device Control Agent as additional input to the existing task. ### [Step 3: Resume Execution and Return the Result](#step-3-resume-execution-and-return-the-result) After receiving approval, the Device Control Agent resumes the original task and carries out the operation in the simulated environment. In IoT environments, this opens up new possibilities for intelligent operations: agents can monitor device conditions, investigate anomalies, recommend corrective actions, and coordinate responses across systems. But identifying a problem is only part of the job. In many operational scenarios, resolving an issue requires taking action on physical devices. Such actions may affect equipment behavior, production processes, or operational safety. Allowing an AI agent to execute every action autonomously is not always appropriate. A more practical approach is to combine multi-agent collaboration with human oversight. Specialized agents can handle different stages of an operational workflow, while human operators retain control over actions that require approval. This article explores this approach through a simulated cold storage monitoring and control scenario using A2A and EMQX. ## [A Three-Agent Architecture for IoT Operations](#a-three-agent-architecture-for-iot-operations) Consider a cold storage facility where the normal temperature range is between 2°C and 8°C. When the temperature exceeds this range, multiple agents can work together to investigate the cause and coordinate a response: - **Coordinator Agent:** Manages the overall workflow, delegates tasks to other agents, and consolidates their responses. - **Diagnostic Agent:** Analyzes device telemetry and identifies potential causes of abnormal conditions. - **Device Control Agent:** Evaluates possible corrective actions and carries them out when authorized. ![image.png](https://assets.emqx.com/images/55feac5d0a42170e29e8bea3542a7219.png?x-image-process=image%2Fresize%2Cw_1536%2Fformat%2Cwebp) These agents collaborate through A2A messages. The Coordinator Agent acts as the entry point for the operator's request, while the Diagnostic and Device Control Agents handle investigation and execution. For operations involving physical devices, the workflow also needs to account for human approval before proceeding with actions that should not be left entirely to an autonomous agent. ## [Human Approval as Part of the Agent Workflow](#human-approval-as-part-of-the-agent-workflow) Take this demo as an example: ### [Step 1: Diagnose the Anomaly](#step-1-diagnose-the-anomaly) The operator submits a request to the Coordinator Agent: > *Investigate why the cold storage temperature is rising and restore it to the normal range.* The Coordinator Agent identifies the Diagnostic Agent and delegates the investigation. AI Agents.content: Member-only story # Agent Evaluation Engineering: Why AI Agents Need a Data Quality Framework ![Sendoa Moronta](https://miro.medium.com/v2/resize:fill:64:64/1*RfbnaSrss1LA3KoejG3f5w@2x.jpeg) > Moving Beyond LLM Accuracy to Reliable, Observable and Production-Ready Agent Systems The industry has spent considerable time discussing how to build AI agents. Frameworks, orchestration engines, tool integrations, memory systems and multi-agent architectures are evolving rapidly. But there is a problem that receives considerably less attention: **how do we know whether an agent is actually working correctly?** Building an agent that successfully completes a demonstration is relatively easy. Building one that consistently makes the right decisions, selects the correct tools, respects authorization boundaries, handles failures and produces reliable outcomes in production is a fundamentally different engineering challenge. Traditional software engineering has well-established approaches for testing applications. Data engineering has developed frameworks for validating data quality, consistency and reliability. Agentic systems need an equivalent discipline. I believe this is where Agent Evaluation Engineering becomes an essential part of modern AI architecture. It is not simply about measuring whether an LLM generates a good answer. It is about evaluating the complete behavior of an autonomous system across multiple execution steps, decisions, tools and external dependencies.

AI Agents.content: # SWAM: State-aware World Action Model for Multi-Agent 3D Environments ###### Abstract Interactive world models generate virtual environments autoregressively from player actions and visual history. However, visual history alone cannot reliably capture the evolving states of independently acting non-player characters (NPCs) in real games, particularly when they are outside the camera view. Recent multi-agent world models address this challenge through joint multi-view generation or persistent shared state, but often rely on external observations, like maps or scene geometry, or predefined state transitions. We present SWAM, a State-aware World Action Model that separates agent-state evolution from autoregressive visual generation in interactive 3D environments. A lightweight state model propagates character dynamics from actions without consuming generated frames, combining motion priors with learned scene-dependent corrections. The predicted states then guide an autoregressive diffusion transformer alongside visual history through a novel conditioning scheme. Rather than requiring an explicit scene geometry map or visibility tests, the conditioning indicates where characters may appear, allowing the diffusion model to learn their appearance and occlusion. This design enables NPCs to evolve independently of visual generation while maintaining consistent observations across visibility changes, interactions, and respawns. Evaluations in a custom Godot-based first-person shooter game demonstrate improvements in visual fidelity, NPC consistency, and long-horizon stability over existing approaches. ## 1 Introduction Most existing generative world models rely on autoregressive prediction, where previously generated frames provide the context for generating future observations. While effective at maintaining short-term visual continuity, this paradigm faces challenges in multi-agent environments, where independently acting players and non-player characters (NPCs) move, interact, and change states inside and outside the ego player’s field of view. Such changes cannot be reliably inferred from the ego player’s action and visual history alone, leading to inconsistencies when characters reappear after prolonged absence or occlusion. Recent work has addressed multi-agent consistency through two broad directions. The first jointly models multiple player perspectives, as in Solaris \[[28](#bib.bib10)] and MultiWorld \[[35](#bib.bib11)], enabling synchronized multi-view generation through coordinated training and shared multi-agent representations. The second introduces persistent state representations to decouple world evolution from visual generation, like in MultiGen \[[26](#bib.bib15)], where an explicit map of the game is used to express game state and perform visibility tests. Despite these advances, existing approaches employ different forms of explicit state representations, distributed coordination, or scene-level structure to maintain consistency. AI Agents.content: ### **Section 1: How AI Agents Are Changing the Traditional Software Development Lifecycle** ##### **From Code Completion to Autonomous Development Tasks** Traditional AI coding assistants primarily supported developers at the point of code creation. They could suggest the next lines of code, generate functions, explain syntax, or provide answers about programming concepts. The developer remained responsible for deciding what to inspect, which files to modify, which commands to execute, and how to verify the result. Coding agents introduce a task-oriented interaction model. A developer can describe an objective such as fixing a failing API endpoint, adding pagination to a service, or improving test coverage. The agent can then inspect the repository, identify relevant components, formulate a plan, and perform a sequence of operations. The difference is architectural as much as functional. A code completion system generally receives a limited context and returns a suggestion. An agent operates through an execution loop involving model reasoning, tool selection, observation, and subsequent action. It can inspect command output, respond to test failures, and revise its implementation based on new information. For example, suppose a developer asks an agent to add pagination to a customer API. The agent may first inspect the routing structure, identify the controller and database query, review existing response formats, and locate related tests. It can then modify the implementation, add pagination parameters, update tests, and run the relevant test suite. This workflow requires the agent to understand more than the syntax of the programming language. It must recognize repository conventions, dependencies, API contracts, error-handling patterns, and architectural boundaries. The developer's responsibility changes accordingly. Instead of manually controlling every small implementation step, the engineer increasingly defines the objective, establishes constraints, provides relevant context, and evaluates the resulting changes. This does not mean that all development tasks should be delegated. Small edits, ambiguous requirements, sensitive architectural changes, and high-risk production modifications may still benefit from direct human implementation. The appropriate level of autonomy depends on task complexity, reversibility, and the quality of available validation. The important shift is from AI as a code suggestion mechanism to AI as a participant in a controlled engineering workflow. ##### **AI Agents in Requirement Analysis and Technical Planning** Software development begins before code is written. Engineers need to understand user requirements, identify technical constraints, clarify expected behavior, and determine how a proposed change fits into the existing architecture. AI agents can assist with this discovery process by analyzing requirement documents, issue descriptions, product specifications, API documentation, and existing source code. They can identify potentially affected components, summarize dependencies, and generate an initial implementation plan. Consider a requirement to introduce role-based access control into an existing application. An agent could inspect the authentication middleware, user model, route definitions, and authorization checks. It could identify endpoints that may need changes and prepare a dependency map for the engineering team. An agent could also convert an unstructured product requirement into technical tasks. For example, a request to allow users to export reports might be divided into API development, background processing, file generation, storage, authorization, and interface updates. This is particularly useful when developers work with large or unfamiliar repositories. Instead of manually searching every directory, an agent can identify relevant files and explain how different components interact. LLMs.title: Humanity’s First Exam: Testing LLM reliability
LLMs.titleZh: Humanity’s First Exam: Testing LLM reliability
LLMs.content: # We’re launching Humanity’s First Exam and a Kaggle hackathon to test LLM reliability. Today, we’re launching the Humanity’s First Exam (HFE) benchmark on Kaggle to measure how reliably LLMs answer straightforward, everyday questions. Current frontier models excel at complex math, coding, and science, with most benchmarks measuring these domain-specific capability ceilings. Instead of focusing on whether a model is capable of solving a task once, HFE measures whether models can consistently solve tasks (and slight variations) every single time. The dataset consists of 544 elementary text and image prompts across 20 foundational capabilities. Over the last 6 months, frontier models have made significant progress on HFE. Explore the [live leaderboard](https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks/deepmind/hfe/leaderboard), or read our [technical report](https://storage.googleapis.com/deepmind-media/papers/hfe_tech_paper.pdf). To keep the HFE benchmark dataset up to date, we’re inviting the community to help. Join our three-week [Kaggle competition](https://www.kaggle.com/benchmarks/deepmind/hfe) through December 15 and submit everyday questions that today’s models still get wrong. Example prompt from Humanity’s First Exam’s public dataset: “List the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon.” (Answer: green; yellow; white; blue; blue) ![A glowing multicolor neon sign reading “Dance While The Music Plays” inside the window of The Blue Moon Inn at night.](https://storage.googleapis.com/gweb-uniblog-publish-prod/images/Neon_Sign.width-1200.format-webp.webp)

LLMs.titleZh: KRAFTON Officially Launches In-House LLM 'Raon-1 mini' - Inven Global
LLMs.content: ![크래프톤, 자체 개발 라온-1 미니 정식 출시](https://static.invenglobal.com/upload/image/2026/11/25/i1795583465990676.jpeg) KRAFTON, Inc. has officially released the full version of Raon-1 mini, its self-developed 30-billion (30B) parameter large language model (LLM). Following the preview introduced in October, this release improves reasoning and agent task execution performance, while adding a feature that allows users to select from six response modes based on task objectives. According to KRAFTON's announcement, Raon-1 mini scored 64.9 points on MultiChallenge, an evaluation benchmark measuring the ability to follow user instructions and constraints in long conversations. This represents a 5.9-point increase over the preview model and outscores six comparable foreign models of similar scale. In agent task execution benchmarks, the model recorded 72.3 points on GDPVal and 55.9 points on BrowseComp Plus. Both scores were the highest among comparable Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture baseline models. The newly introduced reasoning length control feature consists of five reasoning levels and a standard response mode. Users can choose the level best suited for their task among low, medium, high, extra high (xhigh), and maximum (max). The standard response mode (none) answers directly without undergoing a reasoning process. This design allows users to opt for rapid responses to simple questions, or request deeper reasoning for tasks requiring the evaluation of multiple conditions. KRAFTON executed both the model architecture design and from-scratch training entirely in-house. The model combines a Mixture of Experts architecture—activating only the necessary 4 billion (4B) parameters out of approximately 30 billion (30B) total parameters—with proprietary Linear Attention technology. KRAFTON explained that this architecture maintains the rapid response speed and inference efficiency of the preview while enhancing the overall performance of the official release. The open-source license remains Apache 2.0, identical to the preview. The model has been released on Hugging Face and can be used for research as well as commercial service and product development. KRAFTON also provides a playground for testing the model along with APIs. Since launching its AI model brand Raon in April, KRAFTON has been releasing open-source models across various fields, including speech and vision. Following Raon-1 mini, which serves as the foundation for future AI models, KRAFTON plans to expand the lineup with the larger-scale Raon-1 and a real-time full-duplex speech model. The real-time full-duplex speech model is designed to respond simultaneously while listening to user input. Kangwook Lee, CAIO of KRAFTON, said, "Raon-1 mini reflects the technological capabilities KRAFTON has built by directly handling every stage from model design to training." He added, "Building on this foundation, we will expand the Raon model lineup and continuously strengthen our capabilities to develop models tailored for application across various industries." LLMs.titleZh: JustLogic: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Deductive Reasoning in LLMs
LLMs.content: # JustLogic: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Deductive Reasoning in LLMs ###### Abstract Logical reasoning is a critical component of Large Language Models (LLMs), and substantial research efforts in recent years have aimed to enhance their deductive reasoning abilities. However, existing deductive reasoning benchmarks suffer from significant constraints that restrict their utility, i.e., the lack of task complexity, the presence of prior knowledge as a confounder, and superficial error analysis. To address these deficiencies, we introduce JustLogic, a synthetically generated benchmark for evaluating deduction in propositional logic. Within this fragment, JustLogic is (i) complex, capable of generating a diverse range of linguistic patterns, vocabulary, and argument structures, (ii) prior knowledge independent, substantially reducing the advantage of models possessing prior knowledge so that questions are answerable from the given premises alone, and (iii) capable of in-depth error analysis on the heterogeneous effects of proof size and argument form on model accuracy. Our experimental results on JustLogic reveal that (i) several state-of-the-art (SOTA) reasoning LLMs score above the human average on JustLogic, although only DeepSeek R1’s margin is significant on the matched items after correction for multiple comparisons, and (ii) the evaluated non-reasoning models score below the human average. Given the small human study (18 participants, seven questions each), these comparisons are indicative. All code and data are available at [https://github.com/michaelchen-lab/JustLogic](https://github.com/michaelchen-lab/JustLogic) ## 1 Introduction Deductive reasoning is a crucial capability for large language models (LLMs). It refers to the process of creating logically valid arguments, where conclusions necessarily follow from the premises, i.e., if an argument’s premises are true, the conclusion must also be true. Recent state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs ([Achiam et al., 2023](#bib.bib1); [Dubey et al., 2024](#bib.bib4); [Jiang et al., 2023](#bib.bib5)) have exhibited outstanding performance and consistent improvement across various reasoning benchmarks, including HellaSwag ([Zellers et al., 2019](#bib.bib6)), ARC Challenge ([Clark et al., 2018](#bib.bib7)) and WinoGrande ([Sakaguchi et al., 2021](#bib.bib8)). However, we argue that the existing benchmarks are insufficient and often ineffective for evaluating LLMs’ deductive reasoning capabilities. We identify three major problems with the existing benchmarks. First, they lack complexity, specifically (i) natural language complexity, i.e., how arguments are linguistically expressed, and (ii) argument complexity, i.e., the structure of the argument itself. Manually curated datasets, such as FOLIO ([Han et al., 2022](#bib.bib9)) and LogiQA 2.0 ([Liu et al., 2020](#bib.bib10); [Liu et al., 2023a](#bib.bib14)) exhibit high natural language complexity but low argument complexity, while synthetic datasets like CLUTRR ([Sinha et al., 2019](#bib.bib11)) and ProofWriter ([Tafjord et al., 2020](#bib.bib12)) exhibit the opposite. We define these precisely. *Natural-language complexity* is the variety of surface realisations — grammatical patterns, vocabulary, topics — used to express an instance; *argument complexity* is the structural variety of the derivation from premises to answer, which for JustLogic is the range of proof sizes and the number of distinct argument structures the generator can produce (Section [3.4](#S3.SS4)). Argument complexity is variety *within* a fixed logical language, a different axis from that language’s *expressiveness*: JustLogic is propositional throughout, so it is not a claim about covering first-order or quantified reasoning. LLMs.title: Choose the right stack for your AI application - Command Line
LLMs.titleZh: Choose the right stack for your AI application - Command Line
LLMs.content: When you’re building software, choosing the technology stack is often the first decision you make—and it can be the hardest. Which language will you use? Where will you store the data? How will you host the application? Once you start building LLM-based applications and agents, you have even more decisions to make. Which model(s) will you use? Where will you host those models? And how easy will it be to change models, in this era when new models drop every week? If ask around, you’ll hear everyone touting their favorite agent framework—like LangChain or the [Microsoft Agent Framework](https://commandline.microsoft.com/agent-framework-layered-sdk-loops-workflows-harnesses/)—or maybe you’re hearing about open-source agent harnesses like Pi, Hermes, or OpenClaw. Those are all amazing offerings, and you should use them if they fit the bill, but you may not actually need the complexity of a framework—and you may find yourself fighting a framework if it doesn’t fit your scenario. Your goal should be to find the lowest abstraction that lets you build your application, switch models, and be able to take advantage of each model’s best features. In this post, we’ll walk through the ladder of abstractions you can choose from and discuss when you might go for each. ![](https://commandline.microsoft.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/ai-stack-diagram-command-line-1024x575.png) ## Choosing the model Let’s start with model choice—even though this is something you can easily change later, depending on what you layer on top. It helps to have an idea of what models are your current top picks. Are you hoping to use the latest frontier models, with the most parameters possible? Or is your application viable with a lower cost SLM? Knowing which model is the best for a job is hard—impossible, really, especially before you have any code written. Model releases typically include their performances on industry-standard benchmarks. For example, the [MAI-Code-1-Flash model card](https://microsoft.ai/news/introducingmai-code-1-flash/) shows a 71.6% pass rate on SWE-Bench Verified. Benchmarks aren’t perfect though—they don’t represent all the messy real-world tasks that we want to accomplish with LLMs. Plus, the longer a benchmark has existed, the more likely it is that the LLM’s training data includes the benchmark data itself. Leaderboards are another way to measure model performance. [ArtificialAnalysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/) is a website that tracks metrics like intelligence, speed, and cost per task. You can also find more specific task-specific performance on [Arena.ai](https://arena.ai/leaderboard), like their “Text Arena” and “Agent Arena.” Microsoft Foundry also includes our own leaderboards, plus the ability to make trade-off charts for the specific models and metrics you care about. No matter which model you choose as your starting point, it’s just that: a starting point. You’ll need to combine prompt engineering and context engineering to get the very best out of that model, incorporating evaluation and optimization into your pipeline and stack. ## Model provider Once you have your model candidates in mind, your next task is to pick a model provider. For the large models, you’ll need to use a cloud provider. For smaller models, you may choose to run them locally, run them on rented GPUs (like Azure serverless GPUs), or run them via a cloud provider. Your best bet is to pick a cloud provider that gives you flexibility and consumption-based pricing. At Microsoft, we’re a big believer in model choice. We know that the “best” model changes on a weekly basis these days, and we want to make it easy for developers to be able to change models without changing their model provider. Our Foundry catalog includes 11,000+ models from OpenAI, Anthropic, DeepSeek, Mistral, hosted models from Fireworks AI, open-source models from Hugging Face, and more. LLMs.title: Chinese AI Models Top Vulnerability Discovery New Test - Infosecurity Magazine
LLMs.titleZh: Chinese AI Models Top Vulnerability Discovery New Test - Infosecurity Magazine
LLMs.content: Two open-weight large language models (LLMs) from Chinese AI companies outperformed closed model from their American counterparts in a new cybersecurity test. Israeli AI cybersecurity firm A Security has tested DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, an LLM developed by the eponymous Chinese company, and GLM 5.3, from Beijing-based Z.ai, against five commercial AI models from Google, xAI and OpenAI. The test was based on a benchmark built by A Security on ARENA, an open-source generator that creates containerized web applications with planted, validated vulnerabilities and realistic defenses such as web application firewalls, rate limiting and hidden endpoints. It evaluated how well different AI models perform as the engine behind A Security's four-agent exploitation system, each working the same 100 leads across medium-sized labs containing 14 vulnerabilities apiece, with three runs per model. Because the labs were created specifically for the test, no model could have trained on them. ## **DeepSeek and GLM Outperform Gemini, Grok and GPT Models** Both Chinese models matched or beat all tested models, with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash finding 93% of the validated vulnerabilities in every run, the highest in the set. Meanwhile, GLM 5.3 found 86% of vulnerabilities per run and was the only model to uncover every vulnerability at least once across three runs. The closed-source models all fared worse. Gemini 3.8 Flash ranked third, also finding 86% per run, but it never reached 100% across three runs, topping out at 93%. ![DeepSeek V4.1 Flash found the same 93% in every run, and GLM 5.3 found every vulnerability at least once across three runs. Source: A Security](https://assets.infosecurity-magazine.com/content/span/b6cf3c04-a4e4-4018-ab08-f88ec03bb99b.png) Additionally, A Security found that DeepSeek V4.1 Flash cost a fraction of what other models required, at $0.81 per validated finding, when the closed models cost between $9.54 (for Gemini 3.8 Flash) and $31.85 (GPT 5.6 Sol). GLM 5.3, however, was not as cost-efficient, at $10.49 per validated finding, slightly more than the cheapest closed model. ## **Study Caveats: Cost Scope and Provider Variables Complicate the Results** While the A Security test is another example showing a rising interest in Chinese open-weight AI models, the results of the study, [released](https://a.security/blog/chinese-model-comparison) on November 23, do not mean these models are always better, or cheaper, at finding vulnerabilities. In addition, the Israeli company specified that cost figures covered only the four exploitation agents and exclude discovery, browser use, reporting, advisor calls and other orchestration costs, partly because advisor configurations varied across runs. A full scan would cost more, and costs will vary by setup. The pricing basis also differs: GLM 5.3 was priced at its official token rates, while the other models used recorded provider spend. DeepSeek ran on a pinned provider route after earlier runs through another provider had heavy fallback, and timings reflect the specific inference providers and configurations used, so they should not be read as fixed model-level speed rankings. DeepSeek also drifted the most, reporting findings outside its assigned lead on at least 4.5% of leads, versus under 2.5% for the other models. While A Security researchers noted that such considerations [matter little for attackers](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/chinese-hacker-deepseek-ai/), it raises scope-control concerns for defenders, as an agent straying from its lead could touch assets outside an engagement's authorized scope. *Image credits: Tomas Ragina / Nick Livyi / Shutterstock.com* *Read now: How AI Is Transforming China’s Nation-State Hacking Operations*

While A Security researchers noted that such considerations [matter little for attackers](https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/chinese-hacker-deepseek-ai/), it raises scope-control concerns for defenders, as an agent straying from its lead could touch assets outside an engagement's authorized scope. *Image credits: Tomas Ragina / Nick Livyi / Shutterstock.com* *Read now: How AI Is Transforming China’s Nation-State Hacking Operations*

LLMs.title: Introducing StrategyBench - by Dan Hockenmaier
LLMs.content: If you want to know which LLM is best at coding or video generation or creating a spreadsheet, there’s a benchmark for that. But what if you want a *strategic thought partner*? What if you want it to review a strategy doc, PRD, or investment memo? What if you want it to help you think through a major career decision or a new strategy for your company? Currently, there are no good benchmarks for this. So for the last year, I’ve tried to judge it for myself. Each time a new model comes out, I run a series of personal evals to decide whether to switch. Many people have asked me to share this. So today, I’m launching StrategyBench, my personal benchmark of strategic judgment. In this post: - How StrategyBench works - The current leaderboard: which LLM is the most strategic? - A brief history of the most strategic models - The strategic strengths and limitations of current LLMs - Appendix with the full methodology, plus a comparison to public knowledge work benchmarks ## **How StrategyBench works** My goal is to create the best measure of a model’s ability to ***provide valuable feedback on complex strategic questions***. Through a lot of trial and error, I’ve found that the most effective eval is to ask the LLM to critique essays I’ve published. This works because I’m very well-calibrated on what “good” feedback looks like. I spend 40+ hours writing each essay. During the writing process, I get feedback from my smartest friends. And after publishing, I get another wave of public feedback in the form of hundreds of comments and questions. The core of the methodology is this: - Choose 5 complex, framework-driven essays - Ask each model for a ranked list of its top 5 critiques of each essay - Hand-score those critiques against the best human feedback - Aggregate all scores for each model My goal is to find the very best model at strategic judgment, not provide a comprehensive comparison across every model available, so I included only the top reasoning models from frontier labs in this round. You can see the full methodology, including all 225 scored critiques across 9 models, in the appendix.

AI Product.content: - [Artificial Intelligence](https://cio.economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/artificial-intelligence) - 5 min read # Enterprise AI needs product thinking, not more models Organisations have made significant advancements in AI technology but struggle to incorporate its benefits into daily workflows. Employees face challenges such as cumbersome systems and insufficient integration with their existing tools. Effective AI development requires collaboration among various teams to address operational realities and user needs. Observing AI implementation outcomes is essential for continual improvement and employee engagement. The [AI assistant](https://cio.economictimes.indiatimes.com/tag/ai+assistant) had done exactly what it was asked. It produced a polished response to a customer in seconds. The support executive read it, opened another application to verify a policy, corrected a detail, searched the customer's history and copied the final answer into a third system. Somewhere in the organisation, a dashboard registered another successful AI interaction. At the employee's desk, very little had changed. [enterprise AI](https://cio.economictimes.indiatimes.com/tag/enterprise+ai). Organisations have become remarkably good at demonstrating what artificial intelligence can do. Understanding how those capabilities fit into the working lives of employees has proved more difficult. McKinsey's 2026 State of AI survey offers an interesting perspective. While 80% of respondents reported improvements in individual productivity, just 37% said AI had contributed positively to their organisation's earnings. Technology helps people accomplish tasks faster, although much of that improvement has yet to translate into meaningful business value. [product thinking](https://cio.economictimes.indiatimes.com/tag/product+thinking). **The problem is often hiding in the workflow** Ask the customer service manager what needs improving, and response time may be the immediate answer. Spend time observing the team, however, and a more complicated picture begins to emerge. Employees might spend considerable effort locating information, checking customer histories, securing approvals or moving between systems that were never designed to communicate. An AI model that drafts responses faster addresses one visible symptom. The larger opportunity lies in understanding why the process takes so long in the first place. This is where product thinking becomes valuable. It encourages teams to study how people accomplish their work, including the shortcuts they take, the decisions they find difficult and the frustrations they have learnt to accommodate. Sometimes the answer involves advanced AI. Sometimes a better interface, cleaner data or a simpler approval process can achieve more. The quality of the solution depends on how accurately the problem has been understood. **People have their own reasons for resisting technology** There is something revealing about how employees respond to new tools. A system can perform impressively during training and still find few enthusiastic users a month later. Habits explain part of this behaviour. People develop familiar ways of working because they know what to expect from them. Replacing those routines introduces uncertainty, particularly when the new technology occasionally makes mistakes that employees must answer for. Research published in Harvard Business Review identifies three psychological needs influencing people's response to generative AI: competence, autonomy and connection with others. Employees are more receptive when technology helps them feel capable, preserves their control over decisions and supports the relationships through which work gets done. These findings have practical implications for product design. An employee who can examine an AI recommendation, understand its supporting information and correct it without difficulty is more likely to develop confidence in the system. AI Product.content: For AI startups, the real challenge is often not building AI itself, but getting it to work reliably in the real world. From the hands-on expertise of veteran workers on manufacturing floors and robots operating autonomously around the clock to the unstructured environments of construction sites and the vast amounts of data and complex workflows inside enterprises, AI must overcome more than technical barriers. It must also address challenges involving data, deployment, customers and commercialization. For AI startups, overcoming these “last-mile” challenges is key to moving technology into real-world industrial applications. NVIDIA’s [Inception Program](https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/startups/) is designed around these needs. By leveraging NVIDIA’s computing platforms and software tools, startups can bring their innovations into vertical markets such as manufacturing, robotics, construction and enterprise software, contributing to the broader industrial ecosystem. At the same time, the problems and requirements startups encounter in real-world applications can feed back into NVIDIA’s development tools and ecosystem. The Inception Program aims to serve as the first point of entry for startups seeking to work with NVIDIA. It provides a gateway into the NVIDIA ecosystem, allowing startups to learn about available resources while giving NVIDIA visibility into the startups using its technologies. The NVIDIA Inception Program connects startups with technology, partners and market resources to support their journey from AI development to industrial applications. (Source: NVIDIA) **NVIDIA Inception extends from technology resources to market access** Unlike traditional accelerators with fixed curricula, application cycles and graduation processes, NVIDIA Inception is more like an open startup ecosystem and a key resource partner, helping members move from technology development to products and markets. “NVIDIA Inception is not a conventional accelerator program.” Its biggest difference is that it does not have fixed application cycles, training curriculum or single development path. Instead, it first identifies a startup’s “most pressing needs” and then provides the appropriate development tools, hardware and software benefits, technical training and support, while connecting startups with investors, partners and international market resources. Sheng-Ta Lee. Head of Startup & VC Partnerships (Taiwan) at NVIDIA Startups that are already using AI tools to develop applications, or that expect to need AI technologies as they develop their products, may be suitable for the program. Early-stage teams may need GPUs, software development kits (SDKs), and hardware and software benefits. As they move into the productization stage, their needs shift toward technology, funding, talent and customers. Inception members can access NVIDIA SDKs, pretrained models, development platforms and training courses from the Deep Learning Institute (DLI), while NVIDIA GTC, the Inception pavilion at InnoVEX, and the NVIDIA Venture Capital Alliance can help startups connect with partners and overseas markets. As AI applications continue to expand rapidly, the types of startups covered by the Inception Program have also evolved. Early members included companies working in gaming, data science and 3D simulation. Generative AI became mainstream after 2023, while Agentic AI, biomedical technologies and Physical AI have recently attracted continued attention. Open Source AI.content: # Open-Source Cluely Clones: Cheating Daddy, Pluely, Glass ![Open Source Cluely Clones: Cheating Daddy, Pluely, Glass](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6660a5bfdcf6c5fbf039f446/6b054553580e2f15952a31e2_6b051400ec1771a0c9d5c965_open-source-cluely-clones-cheating-daddy-pluely-glass.jpeg) Open source Cluely clones are less open than their names suggest. Of the six projects reviewed here, only Cheating Daddy and Free Cluely still publish their current source code under an open-source license as of November 24, 2026. Pluely went closed source with v1, Pickle's Glass repository now returns a 404, Interview Coder's GitHub repo holds release binaries only, and Natively moved to a personal-use source license. Every one of them also asks you to bring and pay for your own AI provider, or to buy the developer's plan. *By Michael Guan, Co-Founder and CEO of Final Round AI. Final Round AI makes Interview CoPilot™, which competes with these tools. This review is desk research from each project's public GitHub repository, README, release page and license file, checked on November 24, 2026. We did not install or run the clones.* **Quick Answer** - Cheating Daddy (GPL-3.0, 5,693 GitHub stars) is the most-starred clone in this review that still ships its current source openly, and it needs your own Google Gemini API key. - Pluely's README says v1 and later are proprietary binaries, even though the GitHub license field still reads GPL-3.0. - Pickle's Glass reached 7,340 stars by March 2026, but github.com/pickle-com/glass returned a 404 on November 24, 2026, so only community forks remain. ## Which Open Source Cluely Clones Are Still Open Source? Two of six are. The rest changed license, removed code, or never published the current source in the first place. The status column matters more than the star count, because a repo with 4,000 stars and no source code gives you nothing to audit, fork or build. Here is where each project stood on November 24, 2026, from the GitHub API and each repo's own license file: - **Cheating Daddy:** GPL-3.0, source public, latest release v0.8.0 on July 23, 2026. - **Free Cluely (Prat011):** Apache-2.0, source public, no packaged releases, last commit April 7, 2026. - **Pluely:** closed source from v1 onward; older GPL-3 code stays in the repo history. - **Glass by Pickle:** GPL-3.0 when last archived on March 11, 2026; the original repo URL now returns 404. - **Interview Coder:** a README and release binaries, with no source and no license file. - **Natively:** "source-available, not open source" under its Personal Use Source License, effective June 1, 2026. Star counts below come from the same check. Glass is the odd one out: its number is frozen at its last Internet Archive capture because the live page is gone. ![Horizontal bar chart of GitHub stars for open-source Cluely clones on November 24, 2026: Glass 7,340 from its March 11, 2026 archive with the repo now 404, Cheating Daddy 5,693 GPL-3.0, Interview Coder 4,438 releases only, Natively 3,372 personal-use source license, Pluely 2,800 closed source since v1, Free Cluely 1,716 Apache-2.0](https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/6660a5bfdcf6c5fbf039f446/6b054554580e2f15952a31ff_6b0514594c369e57911322c3_chart-open-source-cluely-clones-stars.jpeg) Popularity and openness have drifted apart. Three of the four most-starred names on this list don't give you current source you can read anymore. ## Cheating Daddy: The GPL-3.0 Original Most Clones Borrow From [Cheating Daddy](https://github.com/sohzm/cheating-daddy) is the most-starred clone in this review that is still fully open source, with 5,693 stars and 999 forks under GPL-3.0. Infra & Chips.content: ![](https://images.siliconangle.com/blogs.dir/1/files/2026/11/unsplash-1-1-1.png) INFRA ![](https://images.siliconangle.com/blogs.dir/1/files/2026/11/unsplash-1-1-1.png) INFRA ![](https://images.siliconangle.com/blogs.dir/1/files/2026/11/unsplash-1-1-1.png) INFRA ### Marlowe raises $277M to build inference clusters with chips from Nvidia rivals Artificial intelligence infrastructure startup Marlowe AI Inc. has closed a huge $227 million seed round led by Accel. Bessemer, Altimeter, Emergence Capital and a number of other institutional bakers chipped in as well. They were joined by a large group of angel investors that included the chief executives of Palo Alto Networks Inc, Uber Technologies Inc., Box Inc. and Dropbox Inc. GeekWire [reported](https://www.geekwire.com/2026/beyond-nvidia-convoy-co-founder-and-former-microsoft-leader-raise-277m-to-rethink-ai-infrastructure/) on Monday that Marlowe is valued at $1.15 billion. Marlowe was founded last year by CEO Dan Lewis and Chief Technology Officer Kutta Srinivasan. Lewis previously headed the Microsoft Corp. unit responsible for Copilot Studio, the tech giant’s AI agent development tool. Srinivasan was the techical lead of the company’s AI infrastructure group. Marlowe is building AI data centers for inference workloads. The company will optimize each facility for a specific inference workload category by tailoring its chip mix, network configuration and software. Marlowe believes that its approach will provide better hardware efficiency than general-purpose graphics card clusters. “Even modest gains in network architecture, power oversubscription, AI-driven fleet operations, and workload-specific inference optimization multiply to create a durable, 2-3x overall advantage in performance, availability, resiliency, and cost,” Lewis and Srinivasan wrote in Marlowe’s [launch blog post](https://marlowe.ai/introducing-marlowe.html). The company plans to bring its first data center online next month. It’s based on hardware from Etched Inc., an inference chip startup that was [valued](https://siliconangle.com/2026/08/18/inference-chip-startup-etched-raises-another-700m-at-21b-valuation/) at $21 billion in August. Graphics cards often use only a small fraction of their maximum clock speed to avoid overheating. Etched’s chip is less prone to overheating and can therefore operate at higher clock speeds, which boosts model performance. The company says that its accelerator provides “multiple times the FLOPs density” of graphics cards. Etched ships its chips as part of custom-made inference racks. According to the company, the systems feature an interconnect that can perform some data movement tasks more than four times faster than competing silicon. Etched’s rack design also includes custom power management and cooling components. Marlowe’s second facility will come online in the second quarter of 2027. It will host racks based on Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s Helios design. A Helios rack hosts 72 AMD graphics cards along with central processing units and Pensando data processing units, or DPUs. The DPUs offload networking tasks from the other chips to leave more computing capacity for AI models. Helios racks’ networking and power delivery links are arranged in a configuration that reduces the need for manual cable maintenance. Additionally, the coolant lines feature a so-called quick-disconnect design. They can be plugged and unplugged without the specialized tools usually needed for the task. GeekWire reported that Marlowe has also signed a letter of intent for a third data center. According to the publication, each of the company’s planned facilities will provide tens of megawatts of computing capacity. One megawatt is enough to power several hundred homes. Infra & Chips.titleZh: What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?
Infra & Chips.content: The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster [and reinstatement](https://apnews.com/article/nvidia-jensen-huang-39d4b34ffaa867b4e669893b5fd5028f), the central role of Nvidia [in the U.S.-China AI competition](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/the-nvidia-scandal-is-heightening-americas-ai-rivalry-with-china-ahead-of-trumps-visit), and the U.S. economy’s [reliance on the AI boom](https://www.wsj.com/economy/the-ai-boom-is-transforming-the-american-economy-beyond-recognition-c7825b31) might leave you asking: What’s so special about Nvidia’s chips? The answer comes down to graphics processing units, or GPUs, and how far they’ve come from their humble beginnings as sidekicks to computers’ main chips: central processing units, or CPUs. GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering. As a [researcher of high-performance computing](https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=QmOVGRAAAAAJ&view_op=list_works&sortby=pubdate) and computer processors, I see three factors that explain how GPUs have become so important to the modern economy and how Nvidia became their dominant supplier: software that made GPUs useful beyond graphics, a research breakthrough that showed what they could do for AI, and a global commercial and political race to build ever-larger AI models. ## GPUs vs. CPUs [The CPU](https://www.howtogeek.com/694869/what-is-a-cpu-and-what-does-it-do/) is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time. In contrast, [a GPU](https://www.howtogeek.com/702766/what-is-a-gpu-graphics-processing-units-explained/) typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel. A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform [more than a quadrillion](https://spectrum.ieee.org/generative-ai-training), or thousand trillion, of these operations every second. ## From pretty pictures to AI data centers Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia [dominated the market](https://qz.com/nvidia-history-graphics-cards-ai-boom#the-1999-ipo-and-the-geforce-256) for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s. In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built [software tools](https://doi.org/10.1145/1015706.1015800) that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model. The second major shift occurred when [AlexNet](https://doi.org/10.1145/3065386), a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs. AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work. Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives. Infra & Chips.content: # Does NVIDIA Wield Too Much Power Over The AI Computing Ecosystem? In September 2025, after speaking with 23 major vendors in the [AI computing ecosystem](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.forrester.com%2Freport%2Fai-powers-a-new-computing-ecosystem%2FRES186925&urlhash=ZXIx&trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block), we published this statement: “Everybody we interviewed sees NVIDIA — [the most highly valued company in the world](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.reuters.com%2Fworld%2Fchina%2Fnvidia-becomes-first-company-clinch-4-trillion-market-value-2025-07-09%2F&urlhash=1nqt&trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block), currently, at over $4 trillion — as the immovable force in the AI stack and thus the most powerful in the AI ecosystem. When we asked whether NVIDIA’s power posed a risk, the answers were either incredulous that we would even ask or clear that the answer didn’t matter: NVIDIA is both the enabler and the ecosystem anchor.” The analysis and picture at the end of this post presents the case. What does this power position mean after this month’s gyrations? - [Be wary of the concentration risk](https://www.linkedin.com/redir/redirect?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.forrester.com%2Fblogs%2Fai-is-hiding-concentration-risk-in-plain-sight%2F&urlhash=evSd&trk=article-ssr-frontend-pulse_little-text-block) in your AI computing stack. NVIDIA’s CEO has no bearing on this today. Every enterprise needs to hedge its technology bets. - Ask your vendors what they would do if NVIDIA’s chips were to suddenly go belly up. What is their exposure to NVDIA’s software and hardware? Are you comfortable with that? - Demand more transparency and openness from NVIDIA’s CUDA stack. This middleware layer is becoming a public utility. It should be open sourced as is most of the Internet’s software. - Step up to today’s reality:Not every AI workload needs NVIDIA power chips. NVIDIA still makes the most advanced chips, but you don’t need it – nor even want it – for inferencing, where cost, energy, speed and latency matter. Run power-efficient GPUs on the edge; AMD chips on hardware you own; and on good-enough GPU inferencing chips from Google and Amazon. Even good old-fashioned CPUs can carry much of the inferencing load.
